title: 15 Strange Things on Every Plane, Explained

chapters.name: Intro
sentences: A passenger plane is full of strange little details.
A missing row number. An ashtray on a plane where nobody may smoke. Lights that go dark just before landing.
None of it is random. Every detail has a reason, and some of those reasons were learned the hard way.
Some are about comfort. Some are about money. Most are about safety.
Here are fifteen strange things on every plane, explained.

chapters.name: 1 · White Paint
sentences: Number one. Almost every airliner is painted white.
White reflects sunlight, so the cabin stays cooler on the ground.
Cracks, dents and oil leaks are also much easier to spot on a white surface.
And paint is heavy. On a big jet it can weigh up to twelve hundred pounds, about the same as eight extra passengers on every flight.
Every extra layer of paint means more fuel burned.
So airlines keep the paint light and simple. Dark colors also fade faster in the sun.

chapters.name: 2 · The Left Door
sentences: Number two. You almost always board through the left door.
The habit comes from ships. For centuries, people boarded on the left, the port side, and planes kept the tradition.
It also helps the captain, who sits in the left seat and can line the door up with the jet bridge.
And it keeps you away from the right side, where fuel trucks and baggage loaders are working.
That way, the ground crew can work without passengers in the way.

chapters.name: 3 · No Row 13
sentences: Number three. On many planes, row twelve is followed by row fourteen.
Airlines skip thirteen on purpose, because many people think the number is unlucky.
One big airline said it plainly: rows thirteen and seventeen are missing because they are considered unlucky numbers.
Some skip row seventeen too. In Roman numerals, seventeen can be rearranged into a Latin word that means, my life is over.
The seats are exactly the same. Only the number changes.

chapters.name: 4 · Window Shades
sentences: Number four. For takeoff and landing, the crew asks you to open your window shade.
It is not about the view.
If something goes wrong, the crew must be able to see outside before they open a door.
A fire or smoke on one side means that exit must stay closed, and everyone leaves on the other side.
So the shades stay up during the two riskiest parts of the flight.

chapters.name: 5 · Dim Lights
sentences: Number five. Before a night landing, the cabin lights go dim.
It is not to help you sleep. Boeing data shows that almost half of fatal airliner accidents happen during final approach and landing.
If you have to escape in darkness, your eyes are already used to it.
Your eyes need time to adjust to the dark, and in an emergency there is no time.
Dim light also makes the glowing exit signs easier to see.

chapters.name: 6 · Floor Lights
sentences: Number six. There is a line of small lights along the floor of the aisle.
It exists because of a fire. In nineteen eighty-three, a jet made an emergency landing with its cabin full of thick black smoke.
People could not see the exits above them, and twenty-three did not get out.
Smoke rises. So the lights were put near the floor, where you can still see them, and they lead you to an exit.
The same accident brought smoke detectors to aircraft toilets, and seat cushions that resist fire.

chapters.name: 7 · The Ashtray
sentences: Number seven. Smoking is banned on flights, yet there is still an ashtray by the toilet door.
The ban on smoking in aircraft toilets began in nineteen seventy-three, after a deadly cabin fire near Paris.
By the year two thousand, smoking was banned on every American airline flight.
But the rules still require an ashtray, in case someone breaks the law.
A cigarette thrown into a bin full of paper is the worst thing that could happen. The ashtray gives it a safe place to go.

chapters.name: 8 · Popping Ears
sentences: Number eight. Your ears pop on almost every flight.
Behind your eardrum is a small pocket of air. When the plane climbs or descends, the cabin pressure changes faster than that pocket can keep up.
The difference pushes on your eardrum. That is the pressure you feel.
When you swallow or yawn, a tiny tube opens between your ear and the back of your nose, the pressure evens out, and you hear a pop.
Children have shorter, flatter tubes, which is one reason babies often cry during landing.

chapters.name: 9 · Bland Food
sentences: Number nine. Airplane food often tastes bland, and it is not the chef's fault.
The cabin is pressurized like a mountain eight thousand feet high, and the air is very dry. Both dull your sense of taste and smell.
Researchers found that salty and sweet tastes drop by about thirty percent.
Engine noise matters too. In one study, loud jet noise made sweet things taste weaker, and savory things taste stronger.
Savory tastes survive better, which is why tomato juice is so popular in the air.

chapters.name: 10 · Bending Wings
sentences: Number ten. In turbulence, you can see the wings bending up and down.
That is by design. A wing that flexes takes the load and springs back.
The rules say a wing must survive one and a half times the worst load it should ever meet.
In a test in twenty ten, Boeing bent the wings of a seven eight seven upward by about twenty-five feet. The wing passed.
A stiffer wing would only be heavier, and burn more fuel.

chapters.name: 11 · White Trails
sentences: Number eleven. Some planes draw long white lines across the sky.
It is not smoke. It is mostly ice. Jet exhaust contains water vapor, and at cruising height the air is colder than minus thirty-five degrees.
The vapor freezes into tiny ice crystals.
In dry air the trail vanishes quickly. In humid air it can stay for hours.
It can even spread into thin clouds. So a long trail tells you that the air up high is humid.

chapters.name: 12 · 35,000 Feet
sentences: Number twelve. Airliners cruise at around thirty-five thousand feet, higher than Mount Everest.
Up there the air is thin, so there is less drag, and the plane burns less fuel.
It is also above most of the weather.
But a plane cannot just keep climbing. Too high, and the air is too thin for the wings and the engines. So pilots fly at the sweet spot.
As fuel burns off and the plane gets lighter, they climb a little higher.

chapters.name: 13 · Pilots Repeat
sentences: Number thirteen. Pilots repeat almost everything the control tower tells them.
The habit was written in blood. In nineteen seventy-seven, two jumbo jets collided on a foggy runway in Tenerife, after a radio misunderstanding. Five hundred and eighty-three people died.
It is still the deadliest accident in aviation history.
After that, radio language was made the same everywhere.
The word takeoff is now used only when a plane is truly cleared to go, and crews read key instructions back.

chapters.name: 14 · Jet Blast
sentences: Number fourteen. On the ground, planes keep a wide distance behind each other.
A jet engine works by throwing air backward, very fast.
Even at just forty percent power, a big jet can push air at up to one hundred and twenty miles an hour, as far as two hundred feet behind it.
That is strong enough to flip a small plane. So pilots stay well back, and never point a tail at anyone.
Most jet blast damage is done to other aircraft, especially small, light ones.

chapters.name: 15 · 90 Seconds
chapters.card: HOW FAST CAN YOU GET OUT?
sentences: Number fifteen. Every airliner is designed around ninety seconds.
Aircraft makers must show that a full plane can be emptied in ninety seconds.
In the nineteen eighty-three cabin fire, flames swept through the cabin less than ninety seconds after touchdown.
That is why the aisles, the exits and even the seat cushions are the way they are. The cushions are made to resist fire, to give you those seconds.
It is also why the crew asks you to leave your bags behind.

chapters.name: The End
sentences: So that is fifteen strange things, and fifteen reasons.
Next time you fly, look around. The white paint, the left door, the missing row, the little ashtray.
Almost nothing on a plane is there by accident.
